name: Kriang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gehrmann, Ryan. 2017. The historical phonology of Kriang, a Katuic language. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 10(1): 114-139. hdl:10524/52402 (CC-BY; University of Hawai'i Press). Supporting: Smith, Ronald L. 1973. Reduplication in Ngeq. Mon-Khmer Studies 4: 85-111.
catalog_locator: Gehrmann 2017 sec. 2 'Phonological description', p. 117, second paragraph after the section heading through the first epenthesis sentence. Supporting: Smith 1973 sec. 1.2 'Intonation', p. 88.
catalog_quote: [Gehrmann 2017:117] The canonical Kriang word may be monosyllabic or disyllabic. In disyllabic words, the second syllable, or the main syllable, is stressed and equivalent in its phonotactics to monosyllables. The unstressed first syllable of a disyllabic word, or the presyllable, is deficient in comparison to the main syllable in that its inventory of permissible initial and final consonants is severely limited and in that it does not carry a phonemic vowel. The Kriang phonological word shape may be summarized as follows: (P1(P2)).C1(C2)V(ː)(F) A presyllable must contain a P1 onset but a P2 coda is not required. If no P2 coda is present, an epenthetic central vowel [ɐ] is inserted between P1 and the main syllable onset C1. [Smith 1973:88] In a reduplicated couplet the last syllable of the couplet receives the greatest stress of the word and has the highest intonation of the clause or sentence. The first word or syllable of the couplet is usually on a level tone like the rest of the clause or sentence; the last syllable receives greater stress, higher intonation and longer duration.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: In Ngeq's two-syllable reduplicated descriptive couplets the last syllable carries the greatest stress of the word, together with the highest pitch and longest duration; the first syllable is level like the rest of the clause. This is consistent with the Katuic iambic word template (Gehrmann 2018: 133, main/final syllable always prominent, presyllable always unstressed; Kriang listed in Table 5) and with Chia 2014: 13 (pre-syllables 'typically unstressed'), so word stress falls on the final (main) syllable; no source gives a dedicated stress rule for ordinary non-reduplicated Ngeq words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Smith's statement is restricted to reduplicated adverbial-descriptive couplets and is framed as intonation; he adds (p. 104) that noun reduplications do not change sentence intonation. Chia 2014's 'typically unstressed' for pre-syllables is hedged and cited from Alves 2006 rather than argued for Ngeq.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (the 'stress of the word') for disyllabic descriptive couplets, but tied to clause/sentence intonation (the couplet is the intonation peak of the clause); the Katuic-general statements concern the maximally disyllabic prosodic word. No citation-form or instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the same language ngeq1245 [ngt]: Smith 1973 'Ngeq' (Se Kong river, Saravane province; treats Ngeq, Ngkriang and Khiang as dialects of one language); Chia 2014 'Ngeq (also known as Kriang)' with speakers from villages near Pakse, Champasak; Gehrmann 2017/2018 'Kriang' (Sekong province; dialects Kriang Kaleum and Kriang Tha Taeng). Smith's stress statement is about reduplicated descriptive couplets, not a general word-stress rule.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule 01 (final) for Kriang. Gehrmann's statement that the main = second (final) syllable of the maximally disyllabic word is stressed and the presyllable unstressed is the same placement. It is a general word-level statement from first-hand field work (dialects Kriang Kaleum and Kriang Tha Taeng, description reflecting KTT), so it is stronger than the existing Smith 1973 statement, which concerns only the last syllable of reduplicated adverbial-descriptive couplets. Compared with existing_statements it refines the evidential basis (general word template rather than couplet-specific prominence) while giving the same final placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are at most disyllabic (presyllable + main syllable). The main syllable, which is always the last syllable of the word, carries the stress; the presyllable is unstressed, has no phonemic vowel (only an epenthetic [ɐ]) and a restricted consonant inventory. So stress is on the final (= main) syllable, and monosyllables are stressed trivially.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the paper has no dedicated stress or prosody section, and the word 'stress' occurs only in this one passage. No mention of tone or pitch anywhere; Kriang is treated as a (vocalic) register language (sec. 2.2, pp. 122 ff.), and register is a vowel-phonation contrast, not a stress or tone system.
new_statements.identity_note: Gehrmann 2017 covers both major Kriang dialects, Kriang Kaleum (KK, western Kaleum district) and Kriang Tha Taeng (KTT, Tha Taeng-Sekong road); the author states the two have 'practically identical underlying phonological structures' and that the description and examples reflect KTT unless noted (p. 117). ISO 639-3 ngt is stated in the paper header, matching ngeq1245.
